displayQuote: Do what you can, with what you've got, where you are

meta.title: Who really said "Do what you can, with what you've got, where you are"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Theodore Roosevelt printed this line in his 1913 Autobiography — but credited it to Squire Bill Widener of Virginia. The real source, and the ‘have’ vs ‘got’ mix-up.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Do what you can, with what you've got, where you are'?
meta.ogDescription: Roosevelt wrote it down in 1913 — and credited Squire Bill Widener. Not his own line. Here's the documented source and the common misquote.

answer.label: Not Roosevelt’s own line — he quoted Squire Bill Widener
answer.authorDates: 19th-century farmer of Widener’s Valley, Virginia · quoted by Theodore Roosevelt
answer.sourceLine: The exact words do appear in Theodore Roosevelt’s 1913 Autobiography — but Roosevelt did not claim them. He calls it “a bit of homely philosophy, quoted by Squire Bill Widener, of Widener’s Valley, Virginia.” So the wording is genuine and well-sourced; the popular idea that Roosevelt coined it is the error.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Theodore Roosevelt: An Autobiography, ch. IX (“Outdoors and Indoors”)
Squire Bill Widener, of Widener’s Valley, Virginia
Widely misattributed to Roosevelt as author

source.excerpt: There is a bit of homely philosophy, quoted by Squire Bill Widener, of Widener’s Valley, Virginia, which sums up one’s duty in life: ‘Do what you can, with what you’ve got, where you are.’
trail: Quote Investigator traces the saying to Roosevelt’s 1913 Autobiography and credits Squire Bill Widener, whom Roosevelt names as his source.
The Theodore Roosevelt Center confirms the line is “widely attributed to Theodore Roosevelt” but that he credits it in his Autobiography, ch. IX, to Squire Bill Widener.
Roosevelt’s own wording is “what you’ve got”; the most-shared modern form softens it to “what you have,” per Quote Investigator.
source.excerptNote: From Chapter IX of Roosevelt’s Autobiography. Note that Roosevelt frames the line as something he is quoting, not authoring.
source.rightsNote: The documented source — Roosevelt’s Autobiography — was first published in 1913, well before the 1931 U.S. copyright cutoff, so the text is in the public domain. The saying itself is older folk speech attributed to Squire Bill Widener.

author.name: Squire Bill Widener
author.heading: About Squire Bill Widener
author.metaLine: 19th-century Virginia farmer · the man Roosevelt actually quoted
author.bio: “Squire Bill” Widener was a farmer of Widener’s Valley in southwestern Virginia whom Theodore Roosevelt credited with a line of plain rural wisdom. Almost nothing else about him is documented — he survives in the record chiefly because Roosevelt set his words down in print. The saying is best read as folk philosophy Roosevelt admired and relayed, not a maxim Roosevelt coined.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most repeated Roosevelt “quotes,” and it is not quite his. Roosevelt did write the words — but as a quotation he was passing along, with the credit attached.

items.why: Roosevelt printed the line in his 1913 Autobiography but introduced it as “a bit of homely philosophy, quoted by Squire Bill Widener.” Readers kept the sentence and dropped the credit, per Quote Investigator.
Roosevelt’s text reads “what you’ve got”; the most-circulated version smooths it to “what you have,” a small but real change noted by Quote Investigator.
The saying was linked to Carver in a 1942 newspaper item, one of several later voices who used variants of the same thought, per Quote Investigator.

misattribution.truthLine: The real, documented source is Roosevelt’s 1913 Autobiography, where he quotes Squire Bill Widener — confirmed by the Theodore Roosevelt Center.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line lands like a Roosevelt maxim — terse, bracing, self-reliant — which is exactly why his name stuck to it. But in the Autobiography he is doing something more modest: crediting a plain-spoken Virginia farmer whose wisdom he wanted to preserve.
That small act of attribution is what the internet erased. Strip the “quoted by Squire Bill Widener” clause and you get a clean presidential quotation — tidy, shareable, and slightly false.
context.pull: Roosevelt wrote it down. He also told you it wasn’t his.
